title: Against the Gentrification of the Imaginary: Milu Correch from Villa Urquiza to Gallipoli
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Villa Urquiza, the barrio fills with murals
stops.date_confidence: inferred; Infobae gives no year for the neighbourhood's mural wave, only that it precedes her own first walls
stops.campa: Villa Urquiza is a barrio of low houses and long blank walls in the north of Buenos Aires, and one season those walls begin to fill. Painters arrive with rollers and scaffolding; facades that carried nothing carry figures. Milu Correch lives here. She has painted all her life as a recreation, on paper, at the scale of a hand. Watching her own neighbourhood turn into a gallery she never chose to visit, she falls in love with the format itself: the size of it, the fact that it belongs to whoever walks past. The paper gets bigger after that.
stops.quote: cuando mi barrio de Villa Urquiza se empezó a llenar de murales, me enamoré del formato
stops.quote_source: Infobae, 'Milu Correch, la muralista argentina reconocida en el mundo que pone en la mira al arte urbano', 13 March 2018
suggested_refs: The mural wave in Villa Urquiza, Buenos Aires, in the years before 2013
sources: Infobae, 13 March 2018, interview by Alejo Santander

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the large-format workshop
stops.date_confidence: inferred; La Nacion and Infobae both place the workshop before her first street walls, neither dates it, and no venue is named
stops.campa: She takes a workshop in large format with Leandro Frizzera. The problem it solves is arithmetic before it is art: how a figure drawn on a sheet of A4 becomes a figure several metres high without losing its face. She learns the grid and the plumb line, the trick of stepping back far enough to see what the hand is doing, and never again works small. What she brings to the wall is the figure, not the alphabet of graffiti: bodies and animals and cloth, the ordinary grammar of painting enlarged until a street has to accommodate it.
stops.quote: Me ensañaron a pasar eso que tenés en una hoja A4 a un mural de varios metros.
stops.quote_source: La Nación, 'Las nuevas estrellas del arte', on Leandro Frizzera's large-format workshop
suggested_refs: Leandro Frizzera's large-format mural workshop, Buenos Aires
sources: La Nacion, 'Las nuevas estrellas del arte', nid1643210

stops.name: Villa Urquiza, Queen of the Jungle
stops.date_confidence: attested; the blog post is dated 14 March 2013 and the walls are days older
stops.campa: Her first publicly recorded wall in the city is called Queen of the Jungle. It goes up during Un pueblo, un mural, a muralists' tour crossing Buenos Aires in 2013, and a street art blog photographs it days later alongside work by El Marian, ByGermy and Maria Ajras. No street is named in the record. What survives is the title, the barrio, the month and the photograph, filed by strangers cataloguing a weekend of walls. Whether the wall is still standing is not recorded anywhere.
suggested_refs: buenosairesstreetart.com, 'New designs by El Marian, Milu Correch and ByGermy', 14 March 2013

stops.name: Perpignan, Meeting of Styles
stops.date_confidence: year attested on her own CV; month and day not recorded
stops.campa: Meeting of Styles is a network rather than a festival, a name that travels: the same banner raised in one city after another, walls granted for a weekend, painters who arrive by bus and leave by bus. Correch paints under it at Perpignan, on the French side of the Catalan country, and again at Wiesbaden in Germany the same year. Her own record lists both in a single line, festival and town, nothing else. It is the first year she works outside Argentina, and it is already two countries.
suggested_refs: Meeting of Styles editions at Perpignan and Wiesbaden, 2013

stops.name: Zwickau, the ironworks
stops.date_confidence: year attested on her CV; ibug's own edition list fixes the venue, not the date
stops.campa: Ibug occupies a different derelict building every year and repaints it before the demolition crews or the damp finish it. In 2013 the site is the old ironworks at Zwickau, in Saxony: cold sheds, broken glass, machine beds rusted into the floor. Correch paints inside it. What she paints there is not recorded in any account that survives, not by title and not by photograph. The festival is documented, the venue is documented, and the picture is a gap. She is at the start of a decade in which most of her walls will be remembered only as place names.

stops.name: Paris, the KAT project
stops.date_confidence: year attested on her CV; no month, no address, no press notice
stops.campa: Paris in the same year, for a project her own list names only as KAT. There is no address, no photograph, no press notice. She is a young Argentine painter crossing Europe on invitations rather than commissions, saying yes to a train ticket and a wall in a city she has not seen, and the record of the visit is one line long. The gap is the ordinary condition of the work. A mural belongs to the street it stands on, and the street keeps no archive of its own.

stops.name: Salamanca, Galeria Urbana
stops.date_confidence: year attested on her CV; month and wall unrecorded
stops.campa: Galeria Urbana brings her to Salamanca, sandstone city, university older than any republic she has lived under, its buildings the colour of a held breath. A mural goes up. Its subject is not recorded anywhere. Salamanca and Barcelona in one year, with Perpignan just across the French border, open the country that will call her back more often than any other outside Argentina and Italy: Girona, Valencia, Vigo, Carballo, Cheste, Bueu, Ordes and Fanzara are all still ahead of her.

stops.name: Barcelona, Murs Lliures
stops.date_confidence: year attested on her CV; the free-wall model leaves no wall record
stops.campa: Murs Lliures means free walls, and the model is exactly that: surfaces the city has released, chosen informally, painted without a commission or a client. Correch paints one. Because nobody assigned the wall, nobody recorded which wall it was, and no photograph has surfaced. Barcelona will see her again six years later, but as a name in a collective exhibition rather than a painter on a facade. The free wall and the gallery are two different registers, and she will keep moving between them for the rest of the decade.

stops.name: Mechelen, Mechelen Muurt
stops.date_confidence: year attested on her CV; the festival's own site is gone and cannot corroborate
stops.campa: Mechelen sits between Antwerp and Brussels, a small Flemish city that has decided to become an open-air museum one wall at a time. Correch is invited, paints, and is invited back the following year, one of the programme's repeat names. Two murals a year apart in the same town: whether they answer each other or ignore each other is not recorded, and the festival's own website is gone, its domain now serving advertisements for wall insulation. Belgium will keep calling her, to Louvain-la-Neuve, to Ostend, to the north-west walls.

stops.name: Arce, Memorie Urbane
stops.date_confidence: year attested on her CV; month unrecorded
stops.campa: Memorie Urbane works the small towns of southern Lazio, and in 2015 it brings her to Arce, inland from Frosinone, hills and a castle ruin above terraces of olive. It is her first documented wall in Italy. Italy becomes, over the following eight years, the European country she returns to most: Sapri many times over, then Rome, Torre Pellice, San Potito, Bonito, Lioni, Racale, Airola, Campobasso, Civitacampomarano, Stornara, Montesilvano, Gallipoli. It starts here, on a hill town nobody outside the province names.

stops.name: Sapri, Incipit and Mosaico
stops.date_confidence: year attested on her CV for both the festival wall and the collective show; months unrecorded
stops.campa: Sapri is a small port on the Gulf of Policastro where the Cilento coast turns, a town of a few thousand with a festival called Incipit, meaning the words a book begins with. She paints there, and shows there the same year in a collective called Mosaico. She will come back for the festival in 2016 and 2017, and for a solo exhibition under the festival's own name in 2016 and again in 2018. Six entries, six years, one small town. Nothing in the record explains the attachment; only its length is on paper.
suggested_refs: Incipit festival and the Mosaico collective show, Sapri, 2015

stops.name: Rome, Urban Area
stops.date_confidence: year attested on her CV; no district, no address, no image
stops.campa: Urban Area takes her to Rome, where walls have carried painted figures for two thousand years before she adds one. No neighbourhood, no address and no photograph of the piece has surfaced. Her own list gives the festival and the city and stops there. It is possible to stand today in a Roman suburb in front of a Correch mural and not know it, and equally possible that the wall was buffed within the year. Of all the cities on her list, Rome is the one about which her own record says the least.

stops.name: Louvain-la-Neuve, Kosmopolite Art Tour
stops.date_confidence: year attested on her CV; month and wall unrecorded
stops.campa: Louvain-la-Neuve is a university town built from nothing in the nineteen-seventies, concrete and pedestrian decks laid out across a plateau of Walloon farmland, a place with no old walls at all. The Kosmopolite Art Tour paints its new ones. Correch is on the roster. It is her second Belgian invitation in two years, and the subject of what she painted is not recorded. She is dozens of walls into a practice that leaves almost no paper trail behind it, and the pace is still accelerating.

stops.name: Fundao, the Wool question
stops.date_confidence: CV-only and contested: the festival's own records place every edition in Covilha, not Fundao, and its 2015 programme does not name her
stops.campa: Her own curriculum vitae lists Wool at Fundao, in the Portuguese interior. Wool's own record gives thirteen editions, every one of them in Covilha, sixteen kilometres to the south under the Serra da Estrela, and its 2015 programme names two painters, neither of them her. Both statements stand and neither yields. Something was painted in the Beira Baixa that year, in a region emptying of its people, where a mural is one of the last arguments left for coming to look at a town. The town's name is in dispute.
suggested_refs: WOOL, Covilha Urban Art festival, 2015 programme
sources: woolfest.org, festival history and 2015 edition page

stops.name: Girona, Milestone
stops.date_confidence: year attested on her CV; the El Punt Avui coverage on her press page is undated in the index
stops.campa: Milestone brings her to Girona, the Catalan city stacked above the Onyar with its coloured houses hanging over the water. She paints, and the local paper El Punt Avui runs a piece on the work under the formula that art is making Girona beautiful. Three years later she will name urban beautification as the process she most distrusts being used for. She returns for the same festival in 2018. Girona joins Sapri and Mechelen among the few European towns that call her back to paint a second time.
suggested_refs: El Punt Avui, 'L'art embelleix Girona', indexed on milucorrech.com press page

stops.name: Caldas Street, Villa Ortuzar, the broken umbrella
stops.date_confidence: month attested by the Buenos Aires street art press; the day is not recorded
stops.campa: On a factory wall on Caldas Street, in the workshop-and-warehouse quiet of Villa Ortuzar, she paints a man holding an umbrella that has lost its cloth. Only the ribs are left, spread over his head, protecting nothing. The street is not a tourist circuit and the traffic mostly does not stop. The city's street art press photographs it within weeks. It is the earliest of her walls anywhere to be described in words rather than merely listed, with a street named and a gesture named: a man standing under a skeleton.
suggested_refs: buenosairesstreetart.com, 'Milu Correch latest murals in Villa Ortuzar and Palermo', December 2015

stops.name: Niceto Vega, Palermo Hollywood, Time to Read
stops.date_confidence: reported in December 2015; the painting date is not stated
stops.campa: Niceto Vega runs through Palermo Hollywood, bars and boutiques and night traffic, the opposite of Villa Ortuzar's factory silence. Here she paints a woman lying down and reading, a chain of mice linked around her neck. The title is Time to Read. Thousands will pass it who never learn who painted it. A woman absorbed in a book while small animals move over her body is a figure Correch keeps returning to; a second Palermo wall goes up the same season, and no description of that one survives at all.
suggested_refs: buenosairesstreetart.com, 'Milu Correch latest murals in Villa Ortuzar and Palermo', December 2015

stops.name: Coghlan, the drummers on the garage door
stops.date_confidence: attested; the blog post is dated 13 April 2016 and the wall is newly finished
stops.campa: In Coghlan, a quiet northern barrio of low houses and English street names, she paints the front of a parking garage. Two musicians flank the garage door, drumming; a crow accompanies one of them and a monkey the other. The wall's job is to let cars in and out, and it goes on doing that. The residents did not choose to live beside two drummers and their animals, and now do. The image arrives on a working surface and addresses whoever happens to be walking past.
suggested_refs: buenosairesstreetart.com, 'Milu Correch new mural in Buenos Aires', 13 April 2016

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Coche Bomba
stops.date_confidence: year attested on her CV; no month, and no venue is named in any source, so the city centroid stands in
stops.campa: Coche Bomba, car bomb, is the title she hangs over a solo show in Buenos Aires. No gallery is named anywhere in the record. The same year she holds a second solo show in Sapri under the name Incipit, so the violent title is not even the only room she fills that season. The murals lean toward sleepers and readers and giants; the indoor work takes a sharper name. Whether the contents match the title is unrecoverable: nothing was photographed, catalogued or reviewed in any source that can now be reached.
suggested_refs: Coche Bomba, solo exhibition, Buenos Aires, 2016

stops.name: Bromolla, the porcelain factory
stops.date_confidence: year attested on her CV; months unrecorded for all three Swedish stops
stops.campa: Ifo Center occupies a decommissioned porcelain factory in Bromolla, in the flat south of Sweden, artists installed among the kilns and the sanitary-ware moulds. Correch paints there, and paints at Halmstad on the arena wall and at Nassjo for Arttag the same year. Three Swedish towns in one season, none of them a capital, all of them places where a mural is a civic decision taken by a small council. The far north opens to her in the same months that the Italian south keeps calling her back.

stops.name: Sapri, the solo show
stops.date_confidence: year attested on her CV; month and venue unrecorded
stops.campa: Incipit again, but indoors: a solo exhibition in Sapri under the festival's own name, alongside a further wall for the festival the same year. She has painted the town's walls, shown in its collective, and now fills a room of her own in it. Sapri has a few thousand inhabitants. She will do it once more in 2018. No account records how the invitation began or who in Sapri keeps issuing it, and the pattern is the only evidence of the relationship that has survived at all.

stops.name: Vienna, Calle Libre
stops.date_confidence: year attested on her CV; month, wall and image all unrecorded
stops.campa: Calle Libre is a Spanish name for a festival in a German-speaking capital, and it brings her to Vienna in 2017. She paints once there and never returns. Her list is full of towns that call her back, Sapri, Girona, Mechelen; Vienna does not. Where in the city the wall stands is not stated in any available source, and no photograph of it has surfaced. The invitation is attested, the year is attested, and the image is missing, which by now is the ordinary shape of the record of her work.

stops.name: Fanzara, Miau
stops.date_confidence: year attested on her CV; month unrecorded
stops.campa: Fanzara has a few hundred inhabitants and a festival, Miau, that has painted nearly every house in the village. The town handed its own walls over to outsiders, year after year, until the town itself became the artwork and the buses began to come. Correch adds hers in 2017. What her neighbours for that week made of the image she left on their houses is not recorded, and neither is the image. A village of a few hundred is now a destination, and the houses people live in are the reason the buses come.

stops.name: Helsinki, or Vantaa
stops.date_confidence: year attested on her CV; the CV's city is internally inconsistent, Vantaa and Helsinki being distinct municipalities, so the coordinate is a placeholder
stops.campa: Her list reads Street Art Vantaa, Helsinki, and the two are adjacent Finnish cities rather than one: Vantaa holds the airport, Helsinki the harbour, and the entry does not say which received the wall. Finland appears exactly once in her whole record. The year around it runs Racale, Vienna, Airola, Fanzara, Ahtopol, Quilmes and Belo Horizonte: seven countries on three continents in twelve months, each of them a single line, none of them described. It is the most scattered year of her working life.

stops.name: Belo Horizonte, the gable of a tower
stops.date_confidence: year attested on her CV and corroborated by O Tempo and Infobae; month unrecorded
stops.campa: CURA gives her the gable end of a twenty-eight storey building in Belo Horizonte, the tallest surface she has ever been handed, and a crane to reach it. She works alongside DMS, a graffiti writer of the city, with Dic, Doxs and Pavor also on the festival's walls. Brazil has one of the densest painted-wall cultures on earth, pixacao climbing the same towers by night without permission or crane. She arrives into it as a visiting Argentine on a roster, and leaves behind the largest thing she has ever painted.
stops.quote: Mi último muro en Belo Horizonte en un edificio de 28 pisos de altura
suggested_refs: Circuito Urbano de Arte (CURA), Belo Horizonte, 2017
O Tempo, Cida Falabella, 'Deus e mae'

stops.name: Quilmes, the wall in Los Alamos
stops.date_confidence: the mural is painted in 2017; November is the month of the international selection, not necessarily of the painting
stops.campa: Pinta tu barrio is a municipal programme, not a festival, and it takes her south of the capital to Quilmes, a working city better known nationally for its beer. She paints in the barrio of Los Alamos, for the people who live in Los Alamos. In November a Dutch platform, Street Art Today, names it among the best murals painted anywhere in the world that month, and the wall becomes international news without moving an inch. She is unhappy about the mechanism, and when asked, says so plainly.
stops.quote: Esto pertenece a ese lado sensacionalista de esta disciplina que me incomoda.
suggested_refs: The Los Alamos mural, Quilmes, and the Street Art Today selection of November 2017

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the interview
stops.date_confidence: attested; bylined 13 March 2018, updated 15 March 2018
stops.campa: Infobae comes to her in March 2018 with the news that the world has noticed her, and she declines the frame. The prize is a website's list, she says; had a man from Tucuman paid for the domain, nobody would be asking. Then she goes further, past her own case, and names what she thinks the whole discipline is being used for: urban beautification, the circus set up in front of a nasty and archaic process. She is five years and dozens of walls into a career built entirely on invitations, and she distrusts the machine that issues them.
stops.quote: el capitalismo captura absolutamente todo y eso es inevitable. Creo que es necesario que los actores de esta actividad la repensemos y tomemos, al menos, mínimas posiciones ya que a veces somos el circo de procesos nefastos y arcaicos como el 'embellecimiento urbano'
suggested_refs: Infobae interview by Alejo Santander, 13 March 2018

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Entre Cenizas
stops.date_confidence: contested: Infobae calls it her first exhibition and places it in April of the year of writing, but the article is bylined 13 March 2018, and the title appears nowhere on her own CV
stops.campa: Entre Cenizas, among ashes, is the name of an exhibition Infobae calls her first, though her own list of shows already carries two solo exhibitions from two years earlier and does not carry this title at all. Asked in the same conversation what her work is about, she gives four words and declines to elaborate further. She puts figures several metres high on public walls and leaves the reading to whoever is standing under them. A newspaper is asking her to do that work in advance, and she will not.
stops.quote: De la ambigüedad, de lo que quieras.
stops.quote_source: Infobae, 13 March 2018, answering what her works are about

stops.name: Stavanger, Nuart
stops.date_confidence: year attested on her CV; the Stavanger edition runs in September, but the CV gives no month and no wall
stops.campa: Nuart has run in Stavanger since 2001, built inside a mid-sized Norwegian oil town into one of the most closely watched programmes in the field. An invitation to it functions as a verdict. Correch, five years out from a workshop on how to get an A4 sheet onto a building, receives one. The precise wall is not recorded in any accessible source. What is recorded is the year, and that the festival's Scottish offshoot invites her within the same twelve months, a double call from one programme in one season.

stops.name: Aberdeen, the legends of the region
stops.date_confidence: the 2018 Aberdeen edition runs in April and is confirmed by contemporary coverage; the CV gives only the year
stops.campa: Granite city, North Sea money, a festival in only its second edition. Nuart Aberdeen asks its 2018 painters to work from regional history and legend, and Correch, whose figures already come out of myth and folktale, is handed a Scottish set of them. The wall she painted is not described in any surviving source, but the brief is: she is being asked for a story the city already tells about itself, rendered at the size of a building, by a painter who had never set foot in it.
suggested_refs: This Is Colossal, Nuart Aberdeen recap, 14 May 2018

stops.name: Ostend, The Crystal Ship
stops.date_confidence: the 2018 edition is recapped in May 2018; the CV gives only the year, and the coordinate is the city centre rather than a wall
stops.campa: Ostend is a North Sea port largely rebuilt after the war, and since 2016 it has used murals along its seafront as a deliberate instrument of renewal. The Crystal Ship's 2018 edition is called the largest mural festival in Europe that year, more than fifty interventions in one town. She is one of them. The Belgian press later describes her mooring at Ostend for a third time, a count her own list does not show, and the two records are left standing side by side without a way to choose.
suggested_refs: De Morgen, headline indexed on milucorrech.com press page

stops.name: Carballo, dressing the wall
stops.date_confidence: attested; the La Voz de Galicia piece is dated 25 May 2018 and the work is in progress
stops.campa: Rexenera Fest works Carballo, in the Galician interior behind the Costa da Morte. La Voz de Galicia sends a reporter to watch her paint and files under a verb she uses herself: she is dressing the wall. Not decorating it, not covering it. Dressing it, the way one dresses a body, the building understood as something with a shape underneath that the paint has to fit. It is one of very few occasions in the whole record where a journalist describes her method instead of her itinerary.
suggested_refs: La Voz de Galicia, 'Milu Correch: Vestir con su obra', 25 May 2018

stops.name: Rabat, Jidar
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the CV gives the year only, and no month, wall or image has been recovered for this stop
stops.campa: Jidar means wall in Arabic, and Toiles de Rue means street canvases in French; the festival carries both languages in its name and has been repainting the Hassan and Akkari quarters of Rabat since 2015. It is the only work in Africa anywhere in her record. She arrives into a visual tradition of zellige and calligraphy centuries older than the aerosol can and organised on entirely different principles. What she painted, and where in the city it stands, is not stated in any accessible source.
suggested_refs: Jidar Toiles de Rue, Rabat, 2018 edition

stops.name: Miami Beach, the booth
stops.date_confidence: SCOPE runs during Miami Art Week each December; the CV gives only the year and the city, so the Miami Beach siting is an inference
stops.campa: SCOPE is a satellite fair orbiting Art Basel Miami Beach in the first week of December, tents on the sand off Ocean Drive, collectors circulating with lists. Correch is in a collective show there. It is a different register from a free wall in Fanzara or a garage door in Coghlan: here the work is portable, priced and standing in a booth. She has already said in print that capitalism captures absolutely everything and that this is inevitable. The sentence and the booth belong to the same year of her record.
suggested_refs: SCOPE Art Base, Miami Art Week, December 2018

stops.name: Valencia, Hypatia at the Orriols clinic
stops.date_confidence: the project is reported in May 2019; the CV gives only the year
stops.campa: Murales Interactivos Mujeres de Ciencia is run jointly by the Universitat Politecnica de Valencia, Las Naves and the national science foundation, and it puts scientists onto the walls of public buildings. Correch is given Hypatia of Alexandria, mathematician and astronomer, torn apart by a mob in the year 415. She paints her on the Orriols health centre at Duque de Mandas, with an astrolabe and with lettering drawn from the correspondence that survives about her. A woman killed for her learning, standing sixteen centuries later on a clinic in a working barrio.
suggested_refs: Murales Interactivos Mujeres de Ciencia, Valencia
Centro de salud de Orriols, Duque de Mandas
sources: Valencia Plaza, on the Mujeres de Ciencia project, May 2019

stops.name: La Paz, painting the cemetery
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 2019 by Pagina Siete; the exact day and the wall are not recorded
stops.campa: Natinta paints in the Cementerio General of La Paz, among the niche walls where families keep their dead in stacked tiers and visit them with flowers. The city sits above three thousand metres in a canyon, and the thin air makes an unaccustomed painter work slowly. It is her only documented wall in Bolivia. The festival's name runs close to the natitas, the skulls the city keeps and crowns with flowers each November, though nothing states the connection outright; the Bolivian papers that covered the edition now refuse to serve their pages.
suggested_refs: Pagina Siete, 'El festival de arte urbano Natinta ya pinta el cementerio', 6 November 2019
sources: Pagina Siete, 6 November 2019 (headline only; the article returned HTTP 403)

stops.name: Barracas, Exilio
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: reported 6 May 2019 as finished a couple of weeks earlier, so mid to late April; the exact day is not recorded
stops.campa: On the walls of a workshop in Barracas, tanneries and railway viaducts south of the centre, she paints a doll's face with flames, smoke and a matchbox. The title is Exilio. She works it with Pol Corona, and an air-compressor company underwrites it, which is the arrangement her own list records that year as Sullair Cultura. It is among the last Buenos Aires walls of hers to be documented before the calendar empties. Her whole record for 2020 will contain one line, and that line is a room in Copenhagen.
suggested_refs: buenosairesstreetart.com, 'Milu Correch new mural in Barracas, Buenos Aires', 6 May 2019

stops.name: Rio Grande, the far south
stops.date_confidence: year attested on her CV; month, wall and subject unrecorded
stops.campa: Rio Grande Pinta takes her to Tierra del Fuego, wind off the South Atlantic, a city on one of the last inhabited stretches of the continent. In the same year she paints San Rafael in Mendoza and Monte Grande outside the capital: three Argentine municipal programmes in twelve months, the country crossed corner to corner on public money rather than festival money. What she painted at the end of the world is not described in any source that survives. The distance is the documented fact.
suggested_refs: Rio Grande Pinta, Tierra del Fuego, 2019

stops.name: Copenhagen, JacobaxMilu
stops.date_confidence: year attested on her CV; no month, no venue, and the coordinate is the city centre
stops.campa: A duo show in Copenhagen, her name joined to Jacoba's in the title, is the only entry of any kind in her record for 2020. No wall, no crane, no festival: a room. Everywhere she has painted for seven straight years is closed, and the circuit that carried her through Sweden, Italy, Belgium, Norway, Morocco and Brazil is simply not running. What the two of them showed, and under what premise their names were joined, is not stated anywhere available. The year is one line long and it is indoors.

stops.name: Ordes, the work comes back civic
stops.date_confidence: year attested on her CV; months unrecorded for both Galician stops
stops.campa: Desordes Creativas has painted the small Galician town of Ordes year after year, and in 2021 it is among the first things running again. The same season she paints in Bueu, on the Pontevedra coast, for a project called Violencia Zero. Two Galician towns, both of them commissions with a stated subject rather than free walls. The work comes back slowly and it comes back civic: a mural against violence, a village programme, exactly the register she has always distinguished from the international festival circuit.

stops.name: Stornara, the town of the murals
stops.date_confidence: year attested on her CV; the CV misspells the town, and the identification with Stornara in Puglia is a correction, not a citation
stops.campa: Stornara is a town of a few thousand in the Puglian plain that acquired a street art festival in 2018 and was, within a few years, being called the town of the murals. Correch paints there in 2022. Her own list spells the name wrong, so the town where she worked is misfiled in her own record. The same season carries her to Stigliano in Basilicata, to Bodo above the Arctic Circle for UpNorth, and to Dundalk in Ireland: the touring life restarted at full pace, and the paperwork of it still approximate.

stops.name: Tbilisi, the first wall in the Caucasus
stops.date_confidence: year attested on her CV; month, wall and image unrecorded
stops.campa: Tbilisi Fest brings her to the Caucasus for the first time, into a capital where Soviet-era mosaic and relief work stands alongside a street art scene grown up since independence. The 2023 calendar around it runs nearly as full as her pre-pandemic years: Athens, Montesilvano, Cheste, Vigo, and a book fair at Caa Cati in the Argentine northeast. What she painted in Tbilisi, and on which wall, is not stated in any accessible source. Ten years after Zwickau, the record still consists mostly of place names.

stops.name: Athens, Peramo
stops.date_confidence: year attested on her CV; month and wall unrecorded
stops.campa: Athens has painted walls in permanent argument with each other, political slogans layered over political slogans in the streets below the Acropolis, Exarcheia thickest of all. Peramo brings her into it. A decade separates this wall from the derelict ironworks in Saxony where the touring began, and the shape of the working life between them is legible only as a list: dozens of entries, town after town, most of them undescribed. What she painted in Athens is not recorded either.

stops.name: Gallipoli, against the gentrification of the imaginary
stops.date_confidence: year attested on her own Walls page; no month is given
stops.campa: On a wall in Gallipoli, on the Ionian side of the Salento, she paints something she titles Contra la gentrificacion del imaginario. Against the gentrification of the imaginary. Eight years earlier she had told a newspaper that capitalism captures absolutely everything and that the people doing this work had better take some minimal position about it; the title is that sentence turned into a wall. She is still going up on cranes, and she writes a bilingual newsletter called Brocha y Muro. She is at work.
